pages.text: Maku was in the front seat when Uncle Idris finished his sachet of water. Without thinking, he tossed it out of the window. It landed in the gutter and floated away. “Uncle!” said Maku. “Oh, it is only one sachet,” he laughed. “It is not as if I flooded the city.” Maku did not laugh.
sentences: Maku was in the front seat when Uncle Idris finished his sachet of water.

It landed in the gutter and floated away.
“Uncle!” said Maku.
“Oh, it is only one sachet,” he laughed.
“It is not as if I flooded the city.” Maku did not laugh.
pages.alt: A car on a city road with a hand tossing an empty sachet from the window into a drain.

pages.text: That evening, Maku sat with Grandma Oforiwaa in the compound. Grandma never went to school and could not read a word. But every morning she swept the yard and the street in front of the house, and she cleared the gutter with a hoe. “Why do you do that, Grandma?” asked Maku. “Because it is mine to keep clean,” said Grandma, “and so is the street.”

Grandma never went to school and could not read a word.
But every morning she swept the yard and the street in front of the house, and she cleared the gutter with a hoe.
“Why do you do that, Grandma?” asked Maku.
“Because it is mine to keep clean,” said Grandma, “and so is the street.”
pages.alt: An elderly woman sweeping the yard with a broom of sticks at dawn, with a clean gutter beside her.

pages.text: “When I was young,” said Grandma, “we were told that if you threw rubbish in the gutter, a spirit would catch you at night. We were scared, so we obeyed. But it was a story, not the truth, and when we stopped being afraid, some of us stopped obeying. A lie holds for a while, then it falls. Children deserve the true reasons.” Maku took out her notebook. “Then let us find them.”

We were scared, so we obeyed.
But it was a story, not the truth, and when we stopped being afraid, some of us stopped obeying.
A lie holds for a while, then it falls.
Children deserve the true reasons.” Maku took out her notebook.
“Then let us find them.”
pages.alt: A grandmother and a girl sit under a lamp with a notebook between them.

pages.text: Auntie Pamela, the lawyer, was visiting. “First reason: the law,” she said. “Ghana’s Public Health Act of 2012 makes dumping refuse in unauthorised places an offence. In 2017, twenty-one people in Lapaz were fined seven hundred and twenty cedis each, or six months in jail if they did not pay. The amounts may have changed since then, but the law is there. It is not only a story.”

In 2017, twenty-one people in Lapaz were fined seven hundred and twenty cedis each, or six months in jail if they did not pay.
The amounts may have changed since then, but the law is there.
It is not only a story.”
pages.alt: A courthouse with a notice board listing the offence and a fine, drawn without any person shown.

pages.text: “Second reason: health,” said Auntie Pamela. “From June 2014 to February 2015, more than twenty thousand cases of cholera were recorded in Greater Accra, and 121 people died. A doctor said that a breakdown in waste management was behind it. Dirty water and rubbish can spread diseases that children get most.” Maku shivered. “Those were real people,” she said. “Yes,” said Auntie Pamela.

Dirty water and rubbish can spread diseases that children get most.” Maku shivered.
“Those were real people,” she said.
“Yes,” said Auntie Pamela.
pages.alt: A chart with a line rising steeply and a small glass of clear water beside it.

pages.text: “Third reason: faith,” said Grandma. “Many of us are Christians, Muslims, or follow the old ways. The Bible says God put man in the garden to work it and take care of it. It also tells the old Israelites to bury their waste outside the camp. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, said cleanliness is half of faith. And the Qur’an warns against spreading corruption on the earth. We do not need a spirit in the gutter. We have the word.”

The Bible says God put man in the garden to work it and take care of it.
It also tells the old Israelites to bury their waste outside the camp.
The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, said cleanliness is half of faith.
And the Qur’an warns against spreading corruption on the earth.
We do not need a spirit in the gutter.
We have the word.”
pages.alt: A grandmother with a Bible and a young girl with a prayer cap, both smiling over a clean yard.

pages.text: “Fourth reason: our neighbours,” said Uncle Idris, who had come in quietly. “The Bible tells us to love our neighbour as ourselves, and every religion has something like it. When my sachet blocks a drain, the water may rise in someone else’s home, and the one who loses the most is usually the poor family and the child with nowhere to go. That is not fair. And floods cost our country a great deal of money, which could pay for schools.”

pages.alt: An uncle looks guiltily at a flooded street scene drawn on a page while a girl watches.

pages.text: Uncle Idris stood up. “Maku, would you come with me?” They walked to the gutter, and he picked out his sachet from the day before. “I was wrong,” he said. “It was not about being caught. It was about the true reasons.” Grandma smiled and handed him a broom. “Educated or not,” she said, “rubbish does not read.” Maku wrote it in her notebook and underlined it twice. The end.
